 Big Win Sets Up Democrats To Intensify Probe of Trump’s Obamacare Purge
 By Julie Appleby 
 Nov. 20, 2026 
 Republish 
 The power shift in Congress lends new weight to an investigation into the Trump administration’s cancellation of over 760,000 enrollees’ Affordable Care Act coverage, led partly by Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images) 
 A week before the midterm elections, a dozen Democratic senators sent harshly critical letters to 10 health insurance company CEOs.
 This story also ran on CBS News . It can be republished for free . 
 Why, the letters asked , had those insurers cooperated with what they called a “potentially unlawful” Trump administration effort that resulted in the rapid cancellation of coverage for 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees in late August?
 Then came the Democrats’ stunning electoral sweep that, come January, will put them in control of both the House and Senate. The power shift lends new weight to the insurance investigation , led by Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who is expected to chair the powerful Finance Committee starting next year, and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.
 “Some insurers might view this inquiry as more high-stakes than before given that Democrats will have the power to subpoena documents, hold hearings, and otherwise investigate perceived abuses or missteps,” said Katie Keith, a director of Georgetown University’s Center for Health Policy and the Law.
 “Senator Wyden will continue investigating the secret arrangement between corporate interests and the Trump administration that has deprived Americans of their health care,” Wyden spokesperson Taylor Harvey said in an email. “Senate Democrats will use every tool at their disposal to get answers.”
 New Oversight Muscle 
 For months, the administration has promoted the idea that fraud is rampant in government health programs — from the ACA to Medicaid and hospice — and that the Republican Party is the one to thwart it. The White House and some GOP candidates used this talking point to try to counter Democrats’ campaign messages about affordability.
 The Trump administration’s anti-fraud efforts are ongoing. The August cancellations are part of a larger initiative by the administration to remove from Obamacare plans people who have other coverage and more strictly scrutinize the information people provide to qualify for premium subsidies. Courts blocked some of the administration’s new rules, including heightened income verification for certain low-income enrollees and a moratorium that would have kept up to 19,000 new agents from helping people sign up during the current annual open enrollment period. Ongoing, however, is scrutiny of an additional 419,000 ACA enrollments in a second phase of the cancellation operation.
 Also, new Trump administration requirements compel some people signing up during open enrollment to undergo additional online identity proofing . Insurers were sent guidance in October asking them to look for suspicious patterns among agents and brokers and take action, including cutting commissions, if they found problems. It’s unclear if any insurers have taken those voluntary steps.
 The letters from the Democratic senators to insurers provide a look at what the new majority could pursue in its ongoing inquiry into the administration’s ACA actions.
 Were proper procedures followed for removing people? How many legitimate enrollees were kicked off the rolls? Did the criteria used to target those enrollments — lack of Social Security number or other key data, not having used medical coverage, a full subsidy without a response to outreach efforts — serve as reliable proxies for determining fraud?
 “The tone of these letters underscores just how much of a black box this process was,” said Keith at Georgetown.
 Administration officials, however, have defended the cancellation effort.

 At an Oct. 14 press conference, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz was asked about the initial round of cancellations in late August.
 “That is fraud, we believe,” Oz said . “That is insurance brokers creating, manufacturing accounts without putting Social Security numbers in and has resulted, we have already determined, in 760,000 phantom accounts that we can’t even get in touch with. We call, we write, we send carrier pigeons — like, no one answers.”
 After some of their executives were grilled early in the year over rising healthcare costs, the insurers were given until Nov. 6 to respond to 28 questions from the senators about the cancellation effort, which began in June when they were asked to try to reach more than a million enrollees the administration targeted as suspicious. They handed back to CMS the names of policyholders who did not respond to emails, phone calls, or letters within 30 days.
 The senators sent letters to Elevance Health, Cigna, Oscar Health, AmeriHealth Caritas, Centene, Florida Blue, Health Care Service Corporation, Imperial Insurance Companies, Molina Healthcare, and UnitedHealthcare.
 By Nov. 10, Harvey in Wyden’s office reported “varying levels of responsiveness” from the insurers.
 What Happens Next? 
 Few dispute that there are problems with improper ACA enrollment. This category includes, the administration says , sign-ups with missing or incorrect data; people who fudge their income estimates to get subsidies; “phantom” enrollees, meaning people who either don’t exist or don’t know they have coverage; and those signed up by rogue call centers or agents to garner commissions.
 But there are questions about the relative scale of those problems and the steps by regulators to thwart them.
 “The question is whether they overreached and set up a situation that led to many people who are eligible losing their coverage,” said Chip Kahn, a visiting fellow at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, and the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank. “They will be pushed hard by the new Congress to come up with the goods in terms of making it crystal clear what’s been done, who has been dropped.” Kahn is also the former president and CEO of the Federation of American Hospitals, a trade association of for-profit hospitals.
 The Democratic senators left no doubt about where they stand, saying in their letters that “Republicans are weaponizing fraud falsehoods in order to undercut the ACA Marketplace and kick even more Americans off their health care.”
 But Democrats will face limits if they try to interfere with the purge.
 “Because the cancellation of ACA policies came via executive authority from the Trump administration rather than legislation, they cannot stop the administration from invoking fraud to cancel ACA policies — unless they can find a legislative solution that can survive a presidential veto or is part of a broader budget agreement,” said Jonathan Oberlander , who teaches health policy at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.
 Democrats have said they will move quickly to try to restore the more generous ACA subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, an effort that will face headwinds. But even a failed attempt might play politically with voters as a move to address affordability concerns. The subsidies were designed to make ACA premiums more affordable.
 Marketplace enrollment for 2026 is about 19 million people , down sharply from nearly 22 million in 2025.
 Conservative policy groups maintain that the additional subsidies, put in place during the covid era, fueled fraud by allowing many more people to qualify for fully subsidized plans and encouraging them to fudge income estimates to qualify for the largest credits. Large subsidies that reduced monthly premium payments to $0, they argue, also provided cover for unauthorized sign-ups by rogue brokers.
 “If the subsidies go up and there are more people in zero-premium plans, then absolutely there will be more fraud,” said Brian Blase, president of the conservative Paragon Health Institute, whose reports assert widespread improper enrollments, sometimes basing that on data it says shows that a growing percentage of enrollees don’t use their insurance.
 He’s critical of the Democrats’ letter and expects Congress will ultimately conclude that the administration’s cancellation effort included enough checks to ensure that legitimate enrollees were not caught up or, if they were, could be reinstated.
 Very few people — fewer than 0.01% of those purged — have contacted the federal marketplace to request reinstatement, the CMS press office said in an unsigned email to KFF Health News. The agency has not released further details about the cancellations, including whether everyone who lost coverage is aware.
 Blase is convinced that, eventually, “the Democrats will realize it was commonsense good governance and move on to something else.”
